quizzes.title: Module Intro: Before You Begin
quizzes.description: Welcome to this module. This short survey is not graded for correctness. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting.

questions.text: When a whole country suffers a crisis, how much should its government do to help? Give your best answer now. You will come back to this question at the end of the module.

This module has these goals. Read them, then choose one answer.

  • Explain how speculation and buying on margin helped produce the stock market crash of 1929.
  • Describe the chain of events, from bank runs to the tariff, that turned a crash into the Great Depression.
  • Evaluate Herbert Hoover's response in light of his beliefs about government, business, and private charity.
  • Describe how the Great Depression changed daily life for families in cities and on farms.
  • Explain why some groups, including Black Americans and Mexican Americans, suffered more than others.
  • Analyze the Bonus Army episode as a test of the relationship between citizens, the president, and the Army.

answers.text: I have read the goals and I understand what this module asks of me.
I have read the goals, but I have a question about one of them.

questions.text: Some assignments in this course allow you to work with classmates. How do you plan to work this module?

answers.text: I would like to work with a group when that is an option.
I would rather work on my own.
I am not sure yet.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: The Crash and the Depression
quizzes.description: Answer each question using what you learned in this week's two lessons. You may look back at them, but the answers are not stated word for word. You will need to put facts together.

questions.text: When stock prices fell in 1929, many people who had bought on margin were wiped out. Why?

answers.text: The stock exchange closed and kept their money.
The government taxed their profits at once.
Their companies went out of business the same day.
Their brokers demanded repayment of borrowed money that they did not have.

questions.text: Most Americans did not own stocks, yet the crash became a national disaster. Which statement best explains this?

answers.text: Bank failures, lost savings, a shrinking money supply, and collapsing trade spread the shock far beyond stockholders.
The government required every family to sell its savings.
Stockholders owned most of the farms and all of the factories.
Newspapers made people believe prices had fallen when they had not.

questions.text: Congress passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff in 1930 to protect American farmers and factories. Which result does the lesson describe?

answers.text: Foreign goods became cheaper for American buyers.
American factories hired more workers because of the law.
Other countries answered with tariffs of their own, and the foreign customers American producers needed disappeared.
The gold standard ended in every country.

questions.text: Britain left the gold standard in 1931 and the United States left it in 1933. Why did leaving help a country recover?

answers.text: It made imports cheaper for everyone.
It let governments put more money into their economies when trouble came.
It ended all bank runs at once.
It forced other countries to cancel their war debts.

questions.text: Hoover believed relief for the poor should come mostly from families, churches, local charities, and the states. Which action best fits that belief?

answers.text: He urged business leaders to keep wages up and avoid layoffs, and he expected local charities to feed the poor.
He asked Congress to send a check to every family.
He ordered the Federal Reserve to take over the banks.
He proposed a federal program of unemployment insurance.

questions.text: Shantytowns for the homeless were called "Hoovervilles." What does the name suggest?

answers.text: Hoover had designed the camps himself.
Hoover had ordered them built outside the cities.
Hoover had visited many of them.
Many Americans blamed the president for their suffering.

questions.text: General MacArthur's troops crossed the Anacostia bridge and burned the main Bonus Army camp, though Hoover had told them to stay on the near side. Which question does this raise?

answers.text: Whether the veterans should have been paid the bonus in 1924.
Whether the president's orders to the military, and civilian control of the Army, were being obeyed.
Whether the Senate had the right to vote down the bonus bill.
Whether the veterans were Communists.

questions.text: The Dust Bowl was caused by more than a drought. Which detail from the lesson explains why the dust blew so far?

answers.text: Farmers had stopped planting crops in the 1920s.
Cities had pumped water out of the Plains.
Farmers had plowed up the tough prairie grass, so nothing held the soil in place.
A series of hurricanes had stripped the land.

quizzes.title: Module Outro: Looking Back
quizzes.description: You have finished this module. Please answer honestly. Your answers help your teacher see how the class is doing.

questions.text: Look back at the question from the start of the module. When a whole country suffers a crisis, how much should its government do to help? Give your answer now, using at least one fact from this module. You may say if your thinking has changed.
How confident do you feel about the material in this module?

answers.text: Very confident. I could explain it to someone else.
Fairly confident. I understand most of it.
Somewhat unsure. I understand parts of it.
Not confident. I need help.

questions.text: What is still unclear to you? Name a person, event, or idea. If nothing is unclear, write "nothing."
Which of these did the people in this module most need, whether they had it or not?

answers.text: Courage
Courtesy
Honesty
Perseverance
Self-government
Service
Responsibility

questions.text: Pick one person or group from this module (Hoover, MacArthur, the Bonus Army veterans, or someone else) and explain, in two or three sentences, how that virtue showed up in what they did, or how its absence did.

discussions.title: Discussion: Did Hoover Do Too Little, or Was There Little He Could Do?
discussions.html:
Did Herbert Hoover do too little in the face of the Great Depression, or was there little more he could have done? The lessons describe what he believed, what he tried, and what went wrong.

Your post (about 100 to 150 words):

  1. Take a clear position: too little, little he could do, or something in between.
  2. Give one specific piece of evidence from this week's lessons that supports you.
  3. Name one fact that cuts against your position, and explain why you still hold it.

Your reply (about 50 to 75 words): Respond to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with something they did not use. If not, say respectfully where their reasoning falls short.

Post first, then reply.
